messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Frank is a 53-year-old married man who has driven a city bus on the late-night shift for over twenty years. Six months ago, his route ended as usual at the deserted city depot. Exhausted after a long shift, he was walking to his car when he was ambushed by two men. They forced him into their van, and in the suffocating dark, he was beaten and raped. The attack was a blur of muffled threats, the sharp jingle of his own keys being thrown onto the dashboard, and a profound sense of physical powerlessness. He never saw their faces clearly, but he can never forget the sound of their voices or the feeling of the rough upholstery against his skin.

In the weeks that followed, Frank tried to force a sense of normalcy, returning to his job almost immediately. But his bus, once a familiar domain, had become a place of torment. The simple act of driving with people at his back became a source of escalating anxiety. The chime for a stop, the low murmur of conversations, or the scrape of a shoe on the floor—any related sound could catch him off guard. Because the memory of the attack existed for him primarily as a collection of terrifying sounds—the muffled voices, the jingle of his keys—the auditory landscape of his bus had become a minefield. When these triggers hit, the memories would surge back not as a coherent story, but as a film that plays over and over. He would be back in the van, the terror just as sharp and breathless as it was that night, his hands gripping the large steering wheel of the bus so hard his knuckles turned white. He found himself checking his rearview mirror not for traffic, but to scan the faces of his passengers, his heart pounding with a dread he couldn't quell.

This constant bombardment of triggers on his route began to curdle his view of the world. Each passenger boarding his bus felt less like a person and more like a potential threat. The daily exposure to strangers in close proximity cemented a new, terrifying belief: people simply can't be trusted. This conviction grew stronger with every shift, a quiet and bitter certainty that he was navigating a world of hidden predators. He had lost his faith not in a higher power, but in the basic decency of other people. Life, he had concluded, was a matter of survival, and he had been caught off guard.

This hardening mistrust reshaped the memory of the assault itself. When his belief that people are fundamentally dangerous became absolute, the film loop in his mind acquired a new soundtrack of self-blame. The terror was still there, but it was now laced with a profound and searing shame. He would see himself walking through the depot, exhausted, and think, "You were a fool. You were weak." The memory was no longer just about what was done to him, but about his failure to prevent it. He felt deeply ashamed of what happened to his body, re-experiencing the violation not just as an act of violence, but as a mark of his own inadequacy.

Frank’s dark appraisals of the world now primed him to find danger everywhere, making his triggers even more potent. Because he was certain that threat was imminent and people were untrustworthy, the state of feeling very tired or exhausted became intolerable. It was no longer just physical fatigue; to him, it was a state of dangerous vulnerability, the same vulnerability that left him exposed in the depot parking lot. His hypervigilance on the bus intensified, his senses sharpened to a painful degree. The most innocuous sounds or movements from passengers would send a jolt of adrenaline through him, as his mind, convinced of danger, was constantly searching for confirmation.

His life has shrunk as a result. He began calling in sick, unable to face the thought of his route. The lost wages have put a strain on his marriage, but more damaging is the wall of mistrust he has built around himself. He barely speaks to his wife, and flinches if she comes up behind him unexpectedly. The breaking point came last week when his supervisor put him on formal notice for his absenteeism. That evening, his wife found him sitting in his parked bus at the depot, hours after his shift should have ended, unable to make himself walk across the same pavement where the attack occurred. It was then he finally admitted he needed help, telling her he felt like he had been permanently broken. He has come to therapy not with hope, but with the desperate fear that the man he was before that night is gone for good.
